questions.stem: A student rubs a polythene rod with a cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What has happened during the rubbing process?

options.text: Protons have moved from the cloth to the rod
Electrons have moved from the cloth to the rod
Electrons have moved from the rod to the cloth
Neutrons have moved from the cloth to the rod

questions.explanation: Only electrons can move during charging by friction — protons are fixed in the nucleus and cannot transfer between objects. Since the rod becomes negatively charged, it has gained extra electrons. These electrons must have transferred from the cloth to the rod. Option A is wrong because protons do not move. Option C would make the rod positive, not negative.

questions.stem: Two charged balloons are held near each other. One has a positive charge and the other has a negative charge. What happens when they are released?

options.text: They repel each other and move apart
They attract each other and move together
Nothing happens — only magnets attract and repel
They both fall straight down due to gravity

questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract — a positive charge attracts a negative charge. Like charges repel (positive repels positive, negative repels negative). Option A describes what would happen if both balloons had the same charge. Option C is wrong — electric charges also exert forces on each other, not just magnets.

questions.stem: When refuelling an aircraft, a conducting wire connects the fuel tanker to the aircraft before fuelling begins. Why is this done?

options.text: To make the fuel flow faster
To prevent a static charge building up, which could cause a spark and ignite the fuel
To keep the fuel warm
To measure the amount of fuel being transferred

questions.explanation: Fuel flowing through pipes can generate static charge by friction. If charge builds up, a spark could jump between the tanker and aircraft, igniting the highly flammable fuel vapour. The conducting wire (earthing strap) allows charge to flow safely to earth, preventing dangerous build-up. This is a critical safety application of understanding static electricity.

questions.stem: A positively charged rod is brought near a small piece of uncharged paper. The paper is attracted to the rod. How is this possible if the paper is uncharged?

options.text: The paper becomes negatively charged by contact
The positive rod induces a charge separation in the paper — the near side becomes negative and the far side positive, and the attraction to the near side is stronger
All paper is naturally negative
Gravity pulls the paper towards the rod

questions.explanation: This is electrostatic induction. The positive rod attracts electrons in the paper towards the near side, making it slightly negative, while the far side becomes slightly positive. Since the negative side is closer to the rod, the attractive force is stronger than the repulsive force on the far side, resulting in a net attraction. The paper has not gained or lost charge overall — the charge has simply redistributed.

questions.stem: A Van de Graaff generator transfers charge to a metal dome. A student touches the dome and their hair stands on end. Why does this happen?

options.text: The hair is attracted towards the ceiling by gravity
Static electricity makes the hair magnetic
Each hair strand receives the same type of charge and like charges repel, pushing the hairs apart
The electrical current flowing through the hair heats it up, making it rise

questions.explanation: When charge transfers from the dome to the student, it spreads across their body including each hair strand. All strands receive the same charge (e.g., all positive). Since like charges repel, each strand pushes away from its neighbours, causing the hair to stand on end in all directions. Option B is wrong — static charge and magnetism are different phenomena. Option D is wrong — this is not about current flow or heating.
